newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin aides have limited access to sick Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin aides have limited access to sick Yeltsin.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin's aides are limiting their requests for access to the Russian president to allow him time to prepare for heart surgery, a senior political adviser said on Friday.

Georgy Satarov, describing life in the corridors of power as Yeltsin prepares for an operation late next month, said Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais controlled access to the president but aides were in any case exercising self-restraint.
He said he had not seen the ailing president in person since July and now consulted with him only by sending notes.
Yeltsin's absence had had a big effect on the work of the Kremlin, he said, but played down talk of infighting now that ambitious security chief Alexander Lebed had been fired.
"In theory access to him is not closed, of course, but in this situation the general desire is to let the president prepare quietly for his operation," Satarov told Reuters in an interview.

"When other aides and officials decide when and when not to make written requests, they operate an internal censor in order to bother the president less. We go only with essential information. It is clear that more responsibility lies with us."
He added: "On the whole access is up to Chubais but Chubais also limits himself."

Yeltsin, 65, has hardly appeared in public since he fell ill before the presidential election second round which he won on July 3. He is resting in a sanatorium before a bypass operation due in the second half of November.
Satarov said he had seen Yeltsin "several times" since he was re-elected but the last time was in late July.
"It was a long time ago, in fact at the end of July....We do not meet at the moment. We correspond," he said.
He declined to analyse the impact of Yeltsin's limited contact with his aides but said it had had a "big influence".

Critics say chaos has deepened in Russia because Yeltsin does not have a firm grip on power. His absence has prompted talk of jostling for power in the Kremlin, and Yeltsin himself called for an end to rivalries in a radio address on Friday.

Satarov dismissed the talk of infighting but made clear that Yeltsin's dismissal last week of Lebed, who made enemies by openly stating his desire to become president in his four months in office, had been widely welcomed in the Kremlin.
"You can't say (Lebed hindered) everyone but he complicated things. I can't speak for everyone but those who I know breathed a sigh of relief," Satarov said.

He made clear Chubais was a powerful figure and that it was hard to say if he or Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who has taken on some of Yeltsin's duties temporarily, had more influence in the president's absence.
Chubais and Chernomyrdin have seen Yeltsin more often than any other officials since he fell ill, according to official reports.
Many political analysts say Yeltsin's daughter, Tatyana Dyachenko, is now an important figure in Russian politics. Satarov said her role was limited and denied she had any political influence.

"In the sense that the president does not have a normal work routine at the moment but has a domestic routine, Tatyana Borisovna (Dyachenko) plays the role of a person who reconciles the domestic routine with needs that arise here," he said.
"In that sense you can say that she has influence, but not in any political sense."
